one_liner: Bincode-1.x-compatible Rust serializer with in-place encoding; serializes 3.5-9.6x faster than the prost, FlatBuffers, capnp and rmp-serde crates on log data.
what_it_does: wincode is Anza's (Solana) replacement for bincode 1.x. It produces the same bytes as `bincode::serialize` (fixed-width little-endian integers, u64 sequence lengths, u32 enum tags) as long as your schemas match your serde types. It does not use serde. You derive `SchemaWrite`/`SchemaRead` and call `wincode::serialize`, `serialize_into`, `deserialize` or `serialized_size`. For foreign types you use `#[wincode(with = ...)]` adapters, `containers::*` with pluggable length encodings, or `pod_wrapper!`. A `Configuration` type lets you change byte order, varint encoding, tag width and size limits at compile time.
how_it_is_fast: The main idea is in-place initialization. `SchemaRead::read` writes each field straight into a `MaybeUninit<Dst>`, and `serialize` makes one `size_of` pass, allocates once, and writes into the Vec's spare capacity. There are no staging buffers and none of serde's construct-then-move copies. Each type has a compile-time `TypeMeta` (Static size + zero_copy flag). For static-size types and sequences, it opens an `as_trusted_for` window whose bounds are checked once. For padding-free `#[repr(C)]`/transparent structs, byte arrays and (on little-endian targets) integers and floats, a whole slice becomes a single memcpy, or a borrow of the input. Fixed-width integers keep that memcpy path open. The cost is a bigger wire format.
when_to_use: You already use the bincode 1.x format (Solana accounts, transactions, on-chain data) and want a faster encoder that writes the same bytes.

Payloads are mostly fixed-size or POD data: arrays of f32/u64, `[u8; 32]` hashes and signatures, `#[repr(C)]` structs. Sequences become memcpy. On the mesh dataset it deserializes in 144.44 µs vs 10.253 ms for prost decode.

You want zero-copy borrows (`&[u8]`, `&[u8; N]`, `&PodStruct` via `ZeroCopy::from_bytes`) or in-place mutation of an encoded buffer (`from_bytes_mut`, `deserialize_mut`) without adopting rkyv or FlatBuffers.
Rust-only services where both ends are Rust types and you can write into a reused, pre-sized buffer with `serialize_into`.
no_std targets: `std` and `alloc` are optional features.
when_not_to_use: You need a schema/IDL, cross-language readers, or schema evolution (optional/added fields). The Rust type is the schema, as in bincode, and there is no versioning.

Wire size or bandwidth matters. On log it encodes 1,045,784 bytes vs 703,710 for bitcode, 724,953 for postcard, 784,997 for rmp-serde and 884,628 for prost. The cause is 8-byte fixed lengths on every string. The `VarInt` config shrinks this, but the docs say it hurts speed significantly and disables integer zero-copy.

Your data is string-heavy and speed is the only goal. bitcode beats it on log (96.821 µs vs 137.05 µs serialize, 1.1452 ms vs 1.4166 ms deserialize), and on minecraft_savedata (82.049 µs vs 132.62 µs serialize).
You need a stable API. It is pre-1.0 (0.6.1, Aug 2026): 0.5.0 shipped in March 2026 and 0.6.0 in July. The published audits (Neodyme, OtterSec) cover v0.1.2, not the current code.
Big-endian or non-x86 targets are a priority. Zero-copy of multi-byte integers works only on little-endian, and CI runs on ubuntu-latest (x86-64) only.

integration.dependencies: pastey, thiserror; optional wincode-derive (syn, quote, proc-macro2, darling) via `derive` feature; optional bytes, bv, bumpalo, ecow, indexmap, smallvec, uuid integrations
integration.platforms: any Rust target; no_std supported; integer/float zero-copy only on little-endian; CI tests only on Linux x86-64 (plus Miri)
integration.thread_safety: not documented; the API is stateless free functions and traits over caller-owned buffers
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial: no drop-in for Protobuf, FlatBuffers, Cap'n Proto or MessagePack, since the wire format and the no-IDL model differ. It is close to drop-in for bincode 1.x `bincode::serialize` (same bytes) after you swap serde derives for SchemaWrite/SchemaRead.

gotchas: Every sequence has a default 4 MiB preallocation limit. Deserializing a larger `Vec` (e.g. 4 MiB + 1 byte of `Vec<u8>`) fails with `PreallocationSizeLimit` where bincode succeeds (issues #51, #90). Raise it through `Configuration` or `UseIntLen<_, N>`. The overall deserialization size limit is off by default.

`serialize_into` is not transactional. Dynamic types can leave a partial prefix in the destination buffer, and only static-size types are length-checked up front (issue #418, 'as intended'). Check `serialized_size` first when writing into fixed buffers.

`SchemaWrite`/`SchemaRead` are `unsafe` traits. A wrong manual `TYPE_META` (Static size or zero_copy) or a `pod_wrapper!` on a type with padding or invalid bit patterns is UB. Several unsoundness reports (#79-#82, #89) and an uninitialized-memory leak in `Cursor<Vec>` writers (#306, fixed May 2026) have been closed.
The `tag`/`tag_encoding` enum attributes and `UseIntLen` break bincode byte-compatibility. Trailing bytes are accepted by default.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Choose it over bitcode or postcard when you must stay on the bincode 1.x wire format or want zero-copy/in-place mutation of POD data. bitcode is faster on string-heavy log data and ~33% smaller on the wire. wincode ties it on mk48 (518.04 µs vs 546.49 µs serialize) and is far faster on mesh (147.88 µs vs 1.2265 ms). Against serde-zap, serialize speed is the same on log (137.05 vs 135.54 µs) but wincode deserializes faster (1.4166 vs 1.7212 ms). Choose rkyv when you need to read fields without deserializing at all.
verified_claims_summary: Data comes from djkoloski/rust_serialization_benchmark (run 2026-09-10, rustc 1.100.0-nightly, LLVM 23.1.1, lto, target-cpu=native, criterion, 2-core/4-thread AMD EPYC 9V74 VM). On the log dataset, wincode 0.6.1 `serialize_into` a pre-sized reused buffer took 137.05 µs, against 731.23 µs for prost 0.14.4 encode, 763.63 µs for flatbuffers 25.12.19, 480.15 µs for unpacked capnp 0.27.0 and 1.3179 ms for rmp-serde 1.3.1. Deserialize took 1.4166 ms vs 2.6802 ms for prost decode and 2.3829 ms for rmp-serde. These are the Rust crates for those formats, not the C++ libraries, and FlatBuffers/capnp have no deserialize row because they are zero-copy.
